cover.hook: 5 accounting words every business owner must know
cover.sub: Swipe to learn them in 60 seconds

slides.title: 1. Revenue
slides.body: All the money from sales, before any costs are taken out.

slides.title: 2. Gross profit
slides.body: Revenue minus the direct cost of the goods or services you sold.

slides.title: 3. Net profit
slides.body: What is left after every expense: rent, salaries, interest and tax.

slides.title: 4. Working capital
slides.body: Current assets minus current liabilities. Shows if you can pay the next few months' bills.

slides.title: 5. Depreciation
slides.body: Spreading the cost of an asset, like a machine or laptop, over the years you use it.

caption:
5 accounting words every business owner should understand before talking to their CA.

Revenue, gross profit, net profit, working capital and depreciation, explained simply.

Save this for later. Which term should we explain next?

cover.hook: Your business made a profit. So why is the bank account empty?
cover.sub: Profit and cash are not the same

slides.title: Profit is on paper
slides.body: Your books record a sale the day you invoice, even if the customer hasn't paid.

slides.title: Cash is in the bank
slides.body: Salaries, rent and GST are paid from cash, not from profit.

slides.title: Example
slides.body: You sell ₹5 lakh this month, but customers pay in 90 days. Profit today, cash in 3 months.

slides.title: Fix 1: Collect faster
slides.body: Shorter credit terms, advance payments, and polite reminders before the due date.

slides.title: Fix 2: Keep a buffer
slides.body: Hold at least 3 months of fixed expenses as a cash reserve.

caption:
Most small businesses don't shut down from losses. They shut down because they run out of cash.

Track cash, not just profit.

Save this and share it with a founder. How many days do your customers take to pay?

cover.hook: Salary gone by the 20th? Try this one rule.

slides.title: 50% Needs
slides.body: Rent, EMIs, groceries, school fees, electricity and other bills you can't skip.

slides.title: 30% Wants
slides.body: Eating out, shopping, subscriptions and trips.

slides.title: 20% Savings
slides.body: Emergency fund and long-term goals. Move it out on salary day, before spending.

slides.title: Example: ₹40,000 salary
slides.body:
₹20,000 needs
₹12,000 wants
₹8,000 savings

slides.title: Adjust it
slides.body: If needs are above 50%, cut wants first. The savings part is the one to protect.

caption:
A simple way to stop running out of money before month-end.

50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings. Pay yourself first.

Save this for your next salary day.

cover.hook: You're not busy because of work. You're busy because you don't delegate.

slides.title: Mistake 1: No reason
slides.body: Giving the task without the why. People do better work when they know what it is for.

slides.title: Mistake 2: No deadline
slides.body: "When you get time" usually means never. Give a date.

slides.title: Mistake 3: Taking it back
slides.body: Grabbing the task the first time it goes wrong. Coach once, then let them own it.

slides.title: The 80% rule
slides.body: If someone can do it 80% as well as you, hand it over.

slides.title: Start today
slides.body: List 3 tasks you do every week that someone else could do.

caption:
Growing a business means doing less of it yourself.

Give the reason, give a deadline, and let them own it.

Tag a business owner who does everything alone.

cover.hook: You may be losing GST credit you already paid for

slides.title: 1. Not checking GSTR-2B
slides.body: If your supplier hasn't filed, the credit may not appear. Reconcile every month.

slides.title: 2. Paying suppliers late
slides.body: If you don't pay the supplier within 180 days of the invoice, the credit must be reversed.

slides.title: 3. Blocked credits
slides.body: Some items are blocked, like food and most personal motor vehicles. Check before claiming.

slides.title: 4. Wrong GSTIN
slides.body: A typo in your GSTIN on the purchase invoice can cost you the credit.

slides.title: The fix
slides.body: Monthly GSTR-2B reconciliation, before you file GSTR-3B.

caption:
Input tax credit is money. These 4 mistakes quietly take it away.

Reconcile with GSTR-2B every month before filing GSTR-3B.

Save this. Which mistake have you seen most?

cover.hook: No emergency fund? One hospital bill can wipe out years of savings.

slides.title: How much?
slides.body: At least 6 months of essential expenses. Self-employed? Aim for 9 to 12.

slides.title: Example
slides.body: Monthly needs of ₹30,000 means an emergency fund of ₹1.8 lakh.

slides.title: Where to keep it
slides.body: Somewhere safe and quick to withdraw, not in shares. Liquidity matters more than returns.

slides.title: How to build it
slides.body: Start small. Even ₹2,000 a month on autopay adds up.

slides.title: Only for emergencies
slides.body: Job loss, medical costs, urgent repairs. Not sales or holidays.

caption:
An emergency fund is the base of every financial plan.

Aim for 6 months of essential expenses, kept safe and easy to access.

Save this. How many months do you have covered?

cover.hook: Read a balance sheet in 60 seconds

slides.title: The equation
slides.body: Assets = Liabilities + Equity

slides.title: Assets
slides.body: What the business owns: cash, stock, debtors, machines, property.

slides.title: Liabilities
slides.body: What the business owes: loans, creditors, taxes payable.

slides.title: Equity
slides.body: What belongs to the owners: capital put in plus profits kept in the business.

slides.title: Quick check
slides.body: Compare current assets with current liabilities. More assets means you can pay short-term bills.

caption:
The balance sheet is a snapshot of what a business owns and owes on one date.

Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Always.

Save this for your next accounts class or board meeting.

cover.hook: P&L vs balance sheet: what's the difference?

slides.title: Profit & Loss
slides.body: Shows performance over a period. Did you earn more than you spent this year?

slides.title: Balance sheet
slides.body: Shows position on one date. What do you own and owe today?

slides.title: Think of it like this
slides.body: P&L is a video of the year. The balance sheet is a photo of the last day.

slides.title: How they connect
slides.body: Net profit from the P&L adds to equity on the balance sheet.

slides.title: Read both
slides.body: A profitable P&L with a weak balance sheet can still mean trouble.

caption:
P&L is a video of the year. The balance sheet is a photo of one day.

You need both to understand a business.

Share this with a commerce student.

cover.hook: The 3 golden rules of accounting

slides.title: Personal account
slides.body:
Debit the receiver.
Credit the giver.

slides.title: Real account
slides.body:
Debit what comes in.
Credit what goes out.

slides.title: Nominal account
slides.body:
Debit all expenses and losses.
Credit all incomes and gains.

slides.title: Example: rent paid ₹10,000
slides.body:
Debit Rent (expense)
Credit Cash (goes out)

slides.title: Practise
slides.body: Write 5 entries from your own spending this week using these rules.

caption:
Every journal entry follows these 3 golden rules.

Learn them once and debit and credit stop being confusing.

Save this for exam revision.

cover.hook: Is your GST invoice missing something?
cover.sub: Details a tax invoice should carry

slides.title: Supplier details
slides.body: Name, address and GSTIN of the seller.

slides.title: Invoice basics
slides.body: A unique serial number and the date of issue.

slides.title: Buyer details
slides.body: Name, address and GSTIN of the buyer if registered, and place of supply.

slides.title: Item details
slides.body: Description, HSN or SAC code, quantity, value and discount.

slides.title: Tax details
slides.body: Rate and amount of CGST, SGST or IGST shown separately, plus signature.

caption:
A wrong invoice can cost your customer their input tax credit, and cost you the customer.

Check your template against this list.

Save it and share it with your billing team.

cover.hook: How many units must you sell before you make a profit?

slides.title: The formula
slides.body: Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ (Price - Variable cost per unit)

slides.title: Fixed costs
slides.body: Costs that stay the same each month: rent, salaries, loan EMIs.

slides.title: Variable costs
slides.body: Costs per unit sold: raw material, packing, delivery.

slides.title: Use it
slides.body: Before raising rent or hiring, check how many extra units you'd need to sell.

caption:
Every business should know its break-even number.

Fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.

Save this. Do you know your break-even point?

cover.hook: 5 ratios that show if a business is healthy

slides.title: Current ratio
slides.body: Current assets ÷ current liabilities. Can you pay short-term bills?

slides.title: Quick ratio
slides.body: Same, but without stock. A stricter test of cash strength.

slides.title: Debt to equity
slides.body: Total debt ÷ owners' equity. How much of the business runs on loans?

slides.title: Net profit margin
slides.body: Net profit ÷ revenue × 100. How much you keep from every ₹100 of sales.

slides.title: Return on capital
slides.body: Operating profit ÷ capital employed. Is the money in the business working hard?

caption:
Numbers tell you how a business is really doing.

Start with these 5 ratios and track them every quarter.

Save this. Which ratio do you check most?

cover.hook: Want a better credit score? Start with these 5 habits.
cover.sub: It affects every loan you take

slides.title: 1. Pay on time
slides.body: Even one missed EMI or card payment can pull your score down.

slides.title: 2. Use under 30%
slides.body: Keep card spending below 30% of your credit limit.

slides.title: 3. Don't apply too often
slides.body: Many loan or card applications in a short time can hurt your score.

slides.title: 4. Keep old cards
slides.body: A long credit history helps. Think before closing your oldest card.

slides.title: 5. Check your report
slides.body: Check your credit report at least once a year and dispute any errors.

caption:
A good credit score can mean lower interest on your home loan, car loan or business loan.

Pay on time and keep usage low.

Save this and share it with someone planning a loan.

cover.hook: Are you underpricing without knowing it?

slides.title: 1. Forgetting overheads
slides.body: Rent, salaries and electricity must be in your price, not just material cost.

slides.title: 2. Copying competitors
slides.body: Their costs and quality are not yours. Start from your own numbers.

slides.title: 3. Ignoring your time
slides.body: If you work in the business, pay yourself in the price.

slides.title: 4. Never raising prices
slides.body: Costs rise every year. Review prices at least once a year.

slides.title: Quick check
slides.body: Price - all costs per unit = real profit per unit. Is it enough?

caption:
Busy all month but no profit? Your pricing could be the reason.

Price from your full costs, not from your competitor.

Save this. When did you last raise your prices?

cover.hook: Still using one bank account for business and home?

slides.title: Clear profit
slides.body: Mixed accounts hide how much the business really earns.

slides.title: Easier tax filing
slides.body: Your CA spends less time sorting entries, and you pay less for it.

slides.title: Loans get easier
slides.body: Banks prefer clean business statements when you apply for credit.

slides.title: Pay yourself a salary
slides.body: Transfer a fixed amount to your personal account each month.

slides.title: Start this week
slides.body: Open a current account and run every business receipt and payment through it.

caption:
The simplest accounting habit with the biggest payoff: keep business and personal money apart.

One account for the business, a fixed salary for you.

Share this with a business owner who mixes them.

cover.hook: Long meetings, no results? Try the 15-minute format.

slides.title: Same time daily
slides.body: Pick a fixed time and keep it to 15 minutes. Standing helps.

slides.title: 3 questions each
slides.body: What did you finish? What's next? What is blocking you?

slides.title: Solve later
slides.body: Note problems in the meeting. Fix them after, with only the people involved.

slides.title: One number
slides.body: Share one key number each day: sales, collections or orders.

slides.title: End on time
slides.body: Short meetings that end on time get people to show up.

caption:
Good meetings are short, focused and end on time.

Three questions per person, 15 minutes, every day.

Save this and try it with your team tomorrow.

cover.hook: 30 minutes a week keeps your books clean

slides.title: 1. Record every bill
slides.body: Enter all sales and purchase invoices from the week.

slides.title: 2. Match the bank
slides.body: Tick off each bank entry against your books.

slides.title: 3. Chase payments
slides.body: List customers whose payment is overdue and follow up.

slides.title: 4. Plan payments
slides.body: Note bills due next week so nothing is late.

slides.title: 5. File the papers
slides.body: Store receipts and invoices in one folder, digital or physical.

caption:
Small weekly habits beat a big mess at year-end.

Record, reconcile, chase, plan and file.

Save this checklist and set a weekly reminder.

cover.hook: FIFO or weighted average? How to value your stock

slides.title: FIFO
slides.body: First In, First Out. The oldest stock is treated as sold first.

slides.title: Weighted average
slides.body: Each unit is valued at the average cost of all units held.

slides.title: Example
slides.body:
Bought 10 at ₹100 and 10 at ₹120. Sold 10.
FIFO cost: ₹1,000
Average cost: ₹1,100

slides.title: When prices rise
slides.body: FIFO shows a higher closing stock and higher profit than average cost.

slides.title: Stay consistent
slides.body: Pick one method and use it every year so results can be compared.

caption:
The way you value stock changes your profit.

FIFO vs weighted average, with a simple example.

Save this for your accounts revision.

cover.hook: Cash basis vs accrual basis: which one shows the truth?

slides.title: Cash basis
slides.body: Record income when money is received and expenses when paid.

slides.title: Accrual basis
slides.body: Record income when earned and expenses when incurred, whatever the payment date.

slides.title: Example
slides.body: You finish a ₹50,000 job in March and get paid in April. Accrual: March. Cash: April.

slides.title: Which is better?
slides.body: Accrual shows the true picture of a period. Companies in India must follow it.

slides.title: Tip
slides.body: Even small businesses should track unpaid bills and invoices to see the real position.

caption:
When did you earn it, and when did you get paid? The answer changes your profit.

Cash vs accrual, explained with one example.

Save this and share it with a commerce student.

cover.hook: How long will it take to double your money?

slides.title: The rule
slides.body: Years to double = 72 ÷ yearly return rate

slides.title: At 6%
slides.body: 72 ÷ 6 = about 12 years to double.

slides.title: At 12%
slides.body: 72 ÷ 12 = about 6 years to double.

slides.title: It works for debt too
slides.body: A loan at 24% interest can double what you owe in about 3 years if unpaid.

slides.title: The lesson
slides.body: Start early and avoid high-interest debt. Time does the heavy lifting.

caption:
A simple shortcut to see the power of compounding.

Divide 72 by the interest rate to find the years to double.

Save this. It also shows how fast credit card debt grows.

cover.hook: Customers paying late? 5 ways to get paid faster.

slides.title: 1. Clear terms
slides.body: Write the due date on every invoice, not just "30 days".

slides.title: 2. Invoice the same day
slides.body: Every day you delay the invoice delays the payment.

slides.title: 3. Remind before the due date
slides.body: A polite message 3 days before works better than chasing after.

slides.title: 4. Easy payment
slides.body: Add UPI and bank details on the invoice so paying takes one minute.

slides.title: 5. Small advance
slides.body: For new or slow customers, ask for part payment upfront.

caption:
Your sales are only real when the money is in your bank.

Clear terms, quick invoices and early reminders.

Save this. How long do your customers usually take to pay?

cover.hook: "Grow the business" is not a goal.

slides.title: Specific
slides.body: Say exactly what. "Increase monthly sales", not "do better".

slides.title: Measurable
slides.body: Put a number on it. From ₹5 lakh to ₹6 lakh a month.

slides.title: Achievable
slides.body: Stretch, but stay realistic for your team and budget.

slides.title: Relevant
slides.body: It should matter to where the business is going.

slides.title: Time-bound
slides.body: Set a date. "By 31 March" turns a wish into a plan.

caption:
Vague goals give vague results.

Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

Write one SMART goal for your business in the comments.

cover.hook: Your books and bank don't match? Here's why.

slides.title: 1. Start with balances
slides.body: Note the closing balance in your books and on the bank statement.

slides.title: 2. Cheques not cleared
slides.body: Cheques you issued that the bank hasn't paid yet.

slides.title: 3. Deposits in transit
slides.body: Money you recorded that hasn't reached the bank yet.

slides.title: 4. Bank-only entries
slides.body: Charges, interest and direct credits you haven't recorded.

slides.title: 5. Adjust and match
slides.body: Record the missing entries. Both balances should now agree.

caption:
Bank reconciliation catches errors, missing entries and even fraud.

Do it every month, not once a year.

Save this for your next month-end close.

cover.hook: Fixed cost or variable cost? Know the difference.

slides.title: Fixed costs
slides.body: Stay the same whatever you sell: rent, salaries, insurance.

slides.title: Variable costs
slides.body: Rise with every unit sold: material, packing, delivery, commission.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: High fixed costs mean a quiet month hurts more.

slides.title: Example
slides.body: Rent ₹40,000 is paid whether you sell 10 units or 1,000.

slides.title: Smart move
slides.body: Where you can, turn fixed costs into variable ones, like paying commission instead of salary.

caption:
Knowing which costs are fixed and which are variable helps you price, plan and survive slow months.

Save this and sort your own costs this week.

cover.hook: How much does it cost you to win one customer?

slides.title: CAC
slides.body: Customer acquisition cost = sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers.

slides.title: LTV
slides.body: Lifetime value = average profit per customer over the whole relationship.

slides.title: Example
slides.body: Spend ₹50,000 to win 100 customers. CAC = ₹500.

slides.title: The test
slides.body: If LTV is less than CAC, every new customer loses you money.

slides.title: Improve it
slides.body: Bring customers back with repeat offers. Repeat sales raise LTV.

caption:
Growth only works when each customer is worth more than it costs to win them.

Track CAC and LTV together.

Save this. Do you know your CAC?

cover.hook: Small cash leaks add up to big losses

slides.title: 1. Fixed float
slides.body: Keep a set amount, like ₹5,000, and top it up only to that level.

slides.title: 2. A voucher for everything
slides.body: Every payment needs a voucher and a bill, signed by the person paid.

slides.title: 3. One custodian
slides.body: Only one person handles the cash box.

slides.title: 4. Count weekly
slides.body: Cash in hand + vouchers should always equal the float.

slides.title: 5. Set a limit
slides.body: Anything above a fixed amount should be paid by bank or UPI.

caption:
Petty cash is where small leaks start.

A fixed float, vouchers for everything and weekly counts keep it under control.

Share this with your office manager.

cover.hook: Busy all day, nothing important done?
cover.sub: Sort tasks with the Eisenhower matrix

slides.title: Urgent + Important
slides.body: Do it now. Deadlines, crises, a key client issue.

slides.title: Important, not urgent
slides.body: Schedule it. Planning, learning, building systems. This is where growth happens.

slides.title: Urgent, not important
slides.body: Delegate it. Most calls, routine requests and some emails.

slides.title: Neither
slides.body: Drop it. Endless scrolling and unnecessary meetings.

slides.title: Daily habit
slides.body: Spend the first hour on one important, not urgent task.

caption:
Not everything urgent is important.

Do, schedule, delegate or drop.

Save this and sort tomorrow's to-do list with it.

cover.hook: A 25% markup is not a 25% margin

slides.title: Markup
slides.body:
Profit as a % of cost.
(Price - Cost) ÷ Cost

slides.title: Margin
slides.body:
Profit as a % of selling price.
(Price - Cost) ÷ Price

slides.title: Example
slides.body:
Cost ₹100, price ₹125.
Markup = 25%
Margin = 20%

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: Plan for a 25% margin but add a 25% markup, and you earn less than you planned.

slides.title: Quick rule
slides.body: For a 25% margin, mark up by about 33%.

caption:
Mixing up margin and markup is one of the most common pricing errors.

Markup is on cost. Margin is on price.

Save this and share it with your sales team.

cover.hook: Do you know your numbers before the month ends?

slides.title: 1. Sales
slides.body: This month vs last month vs target.

slides.title: 2. Gross margin
slides.body: Are you keeping the same share of each sale?

slides.title: 3. Expenses
slides.body: Top 5 expenses and any jump over last month.

slides.title: 4. Cash position
slides.body: Bank balance, money to collect and bills to pay.

slides.title: 5. One action
slides.body: End every report with one decision for next month.

caption:
Big companies run on monthly reports. Small businesses can too.

Sales, margin, expenses, cash and one action.

Save this template for your next month-end.

cover.hook: How to read any company's financials in 5 steps

slides.title: 1. Revenue trend
slides.body: Are sales growing year after year?

slides.title: 2. Profit margin
slides.body: Is the business keeping more or less of each ₹100 of sales?

slides.title: 3. Debt
slides.body: Check borrowings on the balance sheet. Rising fast is a warning sign.

slides.title: 4. Cash from operations
slides.body: Profit should turn into cash. If it doesn't, ask why.

slides.title: 5. Notes to accounts
slides.body: The details and surprises are often hidden here.

caption:
Financial statements tell a story if you read them in the right order.

Revenue, margin, debt, cash flow, then the notes.

This is for learning, not a buy or sell call. Save it for later.
